title.value: Waimeru on keeping the weir order off paper

description.value: Interview with a term steward of the nineteenth length on her refusal of the survey's mapping proposal. Waimeru gives a reason for the refusal that is not the one on file.

content.value:
Q. We would like to draw the lengths. It would only be a drawing.

A. A drawing outlasts a term. Mine runs three more years. Your drawing would be a lie in four and a weapon in ten. I said this at the low water and I am saying it again so that it cannot be filed as a proposal I might soften on.

Q. Is the objection to permanence itself?

A. That is what your colleague wrote down and it is a nicer reason than mine.

Q. What is yours?

A. Two corporations at the draining ground held lengths eleven years past their terms by producing a chart a survey left in the sixties and reading it out at every handing on. It took a generation to get the ground back. I am not making a second chart.

Q. Would you name them?

A. I have named them. Write them down. They are not ashamed and neither am I.

Q. You are otherwise very willing.

A. Because the order is in the mouth and the mouth is mine to spend. Ask me anything that dies when I do.

Q. Then: is there anything on the wall you would not want the order to know?

A. The joint cord for forty-one and forty-two was re-knotted after the walk. I did it. The joint failed the walk and I put it right in the record instead of in the wall, and the wall is still wrong, and the next steward will find it in about a year.

consentNote.value: Waimeru consented to the whole record in speech, twice, on separate days, and refused to sign anything, on the ground that a signature is a drawing of a consent and would outlast the consent. She asked that the last answer be held until her term ends, which it has been.
